name: Olympus Mons
fact: The Solar System’s largest known volcano rises from the Tharsis region. Its broad shield spans more than 600 km, built by repeated eruptions over a long volcanic history.

name: Arsia Mons
fact: Arsia is the southernmost of the three aligned Tharsis Montes volcanoes. Its summit caldera records collapse after large volumes of magma drained from beneath the peak.

name: Ascraeus Mons
fact: Ascraeus is the northernmost of the Tharsis Montes trio. Its summit stands on the Tharsis rise, where immense shield volcanoes dominate the horizon.

name: Pavonis Mons
fact: Pavonis sits between Arsia and Ascraeus Mons in the Tharsis Montes chain. The trio’s near north–south alignment follows the immense Tharsis volcanic province.

name: Elysium Mons
fact: Elysium Mons is the largest volcano in Mars’ second major volcanic province. It rises above Elysium Planitia, far from the better-known Tharsis volcanoes.

name: Alba Mons
fact: Alba is Mars’ widest volcano, with an exceptionally low, broad profile spanning roughly 1,600 km. Its gentle slopes contrast with the steep flanks of many shield volcanoes.

name: Melas Chasma
fact: Melas is one of the deepest parts of Valles Marineris, with layered deposits and landslide terrain along its walls. The chasma lies near the canyon system’s center.

name: Candor Chasma
fact: Candor is a major Valles Marineris chasm between Ophir Chasma to the north and Melas Chasma to the south. Its interior contains layered deposits and steep wall slopes.

name: Ophir Chasma
fact: Ophir is the northernmost of the connected Valles Marineris chasms. Its long, steep-walled trough opens into the canyon network near Candor Chasma.

name: Ius Chasma
fact: Ius forms the western end of Valles Marineris, south of Tithonium Chasma. Its branching troughs and landslide deposits expose a complex history of crustal collapse.

name: Hebes Chasma
fact: Hebes is an enclosed canyon: it has no obvious outlet connecting it to the surrounding Valles Marineris system. A striking interior mound preserves layered material within the basin.

name: Tithonium Chasma
fact: Tithonium lies on the northern side of western Valles Marineris, opposite Ius Chasma. Its deep trough and bright interior deposits make it a window into the canyon’s layered geology.

name: Noctis Labyrinthus
fact: “Labyrinth of the Night” is a maze of intersecting valleys at the western end of Valles Marineris. Fault-bounded blocks and collapsed terrain mark the transition toward the great canyon.

name: Gusev
fact: This 158 km impact crater was explored by NASA’s Spirit rover from 2004 to 2010. Spirit found evidence of ancient water-altered rocks near the Columbia Hills inside the crater.

name: Hellas Planitia
fact: Hellas is a vast impact basin in Mars’ southern hemisphere, more than 2,000 km across. Its floor sits so low that atmospheric pressure there is higher than at most Martian surfaces.

name: Argyre Planitia
fact: Argyre is a large southern impact basin ringed by rugged highlands. Outflow channels connect the basin with the broader drainage network that shaped ancient Mars.

name: Isidis Planitia
fact: Isidis is an ancient impact basin east of Syrtis Major. NASA’s Perseverance landing region lies on its western margin, where a river delta once entered Jezero Crater.

name: Utopia Planitia
fact: At roughly 3,300 km across, Utopia is the largest recognized impact basin on Mars. NASA’s Viking 2 lander and China’s Zhurong rover both explored this northern plain.

name: Schiaparelli
fact: This 460 km crater is named for astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli, whose 19th-century Mars maps popularized many surface names. Its floor includes layered deposits and wind-sculpted dunes.

name: Holden
fact: Holden is a roughly 150 km crater with evidence of both an ancient lake and powerful floods. Its western rim contains Uzboi Vallis, a channel that once carried water toward the basin.

name: Endeavour
fact: NASA’s Opportunity rover explored the rim of Endeavour crater for years after driving there from Victoria crater. Its rocks revealed evidence of ancient water flowing through the region.

name: Victoria
fact: Opportunity studied Victoria crater from 2006 to 2008, examining layered rocks exposed in its steep walls. The small crater’s scalloped rim helped reveal how wind and impacts reshape Meridiani Planum.

name: Eberswalde
fact: Eberswalde preserves one of Mars’ clearest fossilized river deltas, laid down where channels once emptied into a crater lake. Its delta-shaped deposits were a candidate landing site for rover exploration.

name: Lyot
fact: At about 50° north, Lyot is the largest impact crater in Mars’ northern lowlands. Channels and sediments on its floor point to episodes when water or debris moved through the basin.

name: Korolev
fact: Korolev is an 82 km crater near Mars’ north pole, famous for a thick deposit of water ice that persists year-round. The ice cap’s bright surface is about 1.8 km deep at its center.

name: Huygens
fact: Huygens is a large ancient crater in the southern highlands. Its heavily eroded rim and infilled floor record a surface modified by impacts, wind, and possible ancient water activity.

name: Kasei Valles
fact: Kasei Valles is a vast outflow-channel system extending about 1,500 km from the Tharsis region toward Chryse Planitia. Catastrophic floods carved its branching channels and streamlined islands.

name: Ares Vallis
fact: Ares Vallis is an ancient outflow channel where NASA’s Pathfinder lander and Sojourner rover arrived in 1997. Streamlined landforms and rocks there preserve evidence of powerful floods.

name: Mawrth Vallis
fact: Mawrth Vallis cuts through some of Mars’ most extensive clay-rich layered rocks. Orbital spectra show minerals formed in the presence of water, making it a key site for studying ancient habitability.

name: Nili Fossae
fact: Nili Fossae is a set of arcuate troughs along the northwestern edge of Isidis basin. The region’s diverse clay minerals and carbonate-bearing rocks preserve evidence of water-rock reactions.

name: Athabasca Valles
fact: Athabasca Valles is a young-looking outflow channel in Elysium Planitia, associated with flood lavas and possible catastrophic water release. Its smooth floor is crossed by distinctive ridges.

name: Planum Boreum
fact: Planum Boreum is the layered north polar plateau, about 1,000 km wide. Its stacked ice and dust layers preserve a climate record shaped by changes in Mars’ orbit and atmosphere.

name: Planum Australe
fact: Planum Australe is Mars’ south polar plateau, capped by layered deposits of water ice and dust. A seasonal layer of frozen carbon dioxide grows and retreats across it each year.

name: Syrtis Major Planum
fact: Syrtis Major is a dark volcanic plateau whose broad shield and caldera complex formed from ancient lava flows. Its eastern edge borders the Isidis impact basin.

name: Arabia Terra
fact: Arabia Terra is an enormous, heavily cratered highland region in Mars’ northern hemisphere. Its eroded landscapes include layered deposits and landforms that may record ancient groundwater activity.

name: Meridiani Planum
fact: NASA’s Opportunity rover worked across Meridiani Planum for nearly 15 years. Hematite-rich spherules and sedimentary layers there showed that liquid water once altered the rocks.

name: Elysium Planitia
fact: Elysium Planitia is a broad volcanic plain and the landing region of NASA’s InSight mission. InSight measured marsquakes there, revealing details of the planet’s interior.

name: Chryse Planitia
fact: Chryse Planitia is a low northern plain reached by NASA’s Viking 1 lander in 1976. Several large outflow channels empty toward it, linking the plain to Mars’ ancient flood history.

name: Terra Cimmeria
fact: Terra Cimmeria is a vast southern highland terrain, heavily marked by ancient impacts. Magnetic measurements show strong crustal remanence here, evidence of Mars’ early global magnetic field.

name: Apollinaris Mons
fact: Apollinaris Mons is an isolated volcano near Gusev crater, rising above the Aeolis region. Its broad edifice and summit caldera point to a long-lived volcanic history.

name: Hecates Tholus
fact: Hecates Tholus is a broad volcanic mountain in the Elysium province. A large summit caldera and surrounding deposits record volcanic collapse and later modification by ice and erosion.

name: Hadriacus Mons
fact: Hadriacus Mons is an eroded volcanic edifice on the northeastern rim of Hellas basin. Nearby channels and deposits suggest that volcanic heat may once have interacted with subsurface ice.

name: Ma'adim Vallis
fact: Ma’adim Vallis is a long channel that runs from the highlands toward Gusev crater. Its size and branching source terrain are consistent with major episodes of flowing water in Mars’ past.

name: Dao Vallis
fact: Dao Vallis begins near the volcanic highlands east of Hellas and runs toward the basin. Its broad channel and tributaries may have formed when volcanic heat released subsurface water.

name: Mangala Valles
fact: Mangala Valles is an outflow-channel network cut into the southern Tharsis region. Its source includes a large chaotic terrain, where collapse likely released water that carved the channels.
